subject: physics

items.q: A mechanic tightens a nut with a spanner. She applies a force of 45 N to the handle at a point 0.30 m from the axis of the nut. The force makes an angle of 70° with the line joining the axis to the point where the force is applied. What is the magnitude of the torque of this force about the axis?
items.why:
Students meet W = Fs cos θ first and carry the cosine across to the next equation with the same letters. Diagrams often mark the angle between the force and the perpendicular instead of the lever, so the angle is taken from the wrong line. Only the component of the force perpendicular to the line from the axis, F sin θ, turns the body. When the force points straight along the lever (θ = 0°) it produces no torque, and sin 0° = 0 gives this; cos 0° = 1 would wrongly give the maximum torque.

Working: τ = Fr sin θ = (45 N)(0.30 m)(sin 70°) = 13.5 N m × 0.940 = 12.7 N m.
items.specStatementText: the torque τ of a force about an axis as given by τ = Fr sin θ

items.q: A rigid body is free to turn about a fixed axis. One of the forces acting on it lies in a plane perpendicular to the axis. Under which condition is the torque of this force about the axis zero?
items.correct: Its line of action passes through the axis of rotation.
items.misconception: The body remains at rest while this force acts on it.
items.why: Everyday language links 'turning effect' to visible turning, and students carry over the idea that forces are only present when motion happens, the rotational form of 'motion implies force'. Torque is a property of a force and its position relative to an axis, τ = Fr sin θ. A body at rest can have several large torques acting on it that cancel, as in a balanced see-saw.
items.specStatementText: the torque τ of a force about an axis as given by τ = Fr sin θ
items.random_wrong: It acts perpendicular to the line from the axis to where it acts.

items.q: A uniform plank of length 4.0 m and weight 150 N rests on a pivot 1.2 m from end A. A load of weight 90 N hangs from the other end, B. The weight of the plank acts at its midpoint. What weight must hang from end A for the plank to rest horizontally in equilibrium?
items.why:
Introductory problems use 'light' rods and beams of negligible mass, so students learn to list only the loads and forget that a real beam has weight. Treat the beam's weight as a single force acting at its centre of mass (the midpoint of a uniform beam). Its torque about the pivot is its weight multiplied by the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass.

Working: Take torques about the pivot (the pivot force then has no torque). Midpoint is 2.0 m from A, i.e. 0.80 m from the pivot on the B side; B is 2.8 m from the pivot. Torque in the B sense: (150 N)(0.80 m) + (90 N)(2.8 m) = 120 + 252 = 372 N m. Torque in the A sense: W(1.2 m). Rotational equilibrium: 1.2W = 372, so W = 310 N.
items.specStatementText: that bodies in rotational equilibrium have a resultant torque of zero
items.working: Take torques about the pivot (the pivot force then has no torque). Midpoint is 2.0 m from A, i.e. 0.80 m from the pivot on the B side; B is 2.8 m from the pivot. Torque in the B sense: (150 N)(0.80 m) + (90 N)(2.8 m) = 120 + 252 = 372 N m. Torque in the A sense: W(1.2 m). Rotational equilibrium: 1.2W = 372, so W = 310 N.

items.q: A rigid body is in rotational equilibrium. Which statement about the body must be true?
items.correct: The resultant torque acting on the body is zero.
items.misconception: The body is not rotating about any axis.
items.why: Equilibrium problems in class are almost always static (balanced beams and see-saws), and in everyday language 'balanced' suggests 'still'. Zero resultant torque means the angular velocity does not change, just as zero resultant force means the linear velocity does not change. A wheel spinning at constant angular speed on a frictionless axle is in rotational equilibrium.
items.specStatementText: that bodies in rotational equilibrium have a resultant torque of zero
items.random_wrong: The forces on each side of its axis are equal.

items.q: A uniform bar lies at rest on frictionless horizontal ice. Two horizontal forces of equal, constant magnitude are then applied, one at each end of the bar, in opposite directions; each force is kept perpendicular to the bar at all times. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement about the bar while the forces act is correct?
items.correct: Its angular speed increases steadily.
items.misconception: It stays at rest and does not turn.
items.why: Equilibrium is first met for particles, where zero resultant force is the whole condition (Newton's first law). Students carry 'balanced forces mean no change in motion' over to extended bodies without adding the torque condition. An extended body is in equilibrium only when both the resultant force and the resultant torque are zero. Check the two conditions separately: a pair of equal, opposite forces acting along different lines gives zero resultant force but a resultant torque.
items.specStatementText: that an unbalanced torque applied to an extended, rigid body will cause angular acceleration
items.random_wrong: It rotates at a constant angular speed.

items.q: A wheel is mounted on a frictionless axle. Starting from rest, a constant resultant torque acts on it for a few seconds and is then removed. How does the wheel move after the torque is removed?
items.correct: It keeps rotating at a constant angular speed.
items.misconception: It slows down steadily and then stops rotating.
items.why: Real wheels and fans slow down when their motor is switched off, and turn steadily while it runs, because friction exerts a torque; the friction is invisible, so the steady turning and the slowing are both credited to the drive. It is the rotational form of 'motion requires a force', with the force taken to be proportional to the speed. Newton's first law has a rotational counterpart: a body continues to rotate at constant angular speed unless an unbalanced torque acts. Everyday wheels stop because of a frictional torque, not because nothing is driving them.
items.specStatementText: that an unbalanced torque applied to an extended, rigid body will cause angular acceleration
items.random_wrong: Its angular speed rises until the torque is used up.

items.q: A bicycle travels along a level road at a constant 7.0 m s⁻¹. Its wheels, each of diameter 0.70 m, roll without slipping. What is the angular speed of each wheel?
items.correct: 20.0 rad s⁻¹
items.misconception: 10.0 rad s⁻¹
items.why:
Wheel and pulley sizes are usually quoted as diameters, and students copy the number given into the equation without checking which distance it is. Always identify r as the distance from the axis to the point concerned. A wheel of diameter 0.70 m has r = 0.35 m at its rim.

Working: Rolling without slipping: v = ωr, r = 0.70 m/2 = 0.35 m. ω = v/r = (7.0 m s⁻¹)/(0.35 m) = 20.0 rad s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that the rotation of a body can be described in terms of angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration
items.random_wrong: 3.18 rad s⁻¹
items.working: Rolling without slipping: v = ωr, r = 0.70 m/2 = 0.35 m. ω = v/r = (7.0 m s⁻¹)/(0.35 m) = 20.0 rad s⁻¹.

items.q: A rigid disc rotates at a steady rate about a fixed axis through its centre. Point P on the disc is 0.10 m from the axis and point Q is 0.20 m from the axis. How do the motions of P and Q compare?
items.correct: Same angular velocity; Q has twice the linear speed of P.
items.misconception: Q has twice the angular velocity and twice the linear speed.
items.why: Everyday language uses 'speed' and 'fast' for both, and students meet v = ωr in circular motion before they have a clear picture of ω as a property of the whole body. Keep the two quantities and their units separate. Convert with v = ωr, which requires the radius; ω and v are numerically equal only for the special case r = 1 m.
items.specStatementText: that the rotation of a body can be described in terms of angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration
items.random_wrong: Both have the same angular velocity and the same linear speed.

items.q: A flywheel rotating at 1500 revolutions per minute is brought to rest with uniform angular deceleration in 20 s. Through what angular displacement does it turn while stopping? (1 revolution = 2π rad.)
items.why:
Δθ = ωt is the first rotational relationship students learn, for uniform circular motion, and they carry it into accelerated rotation without noticing that ω is no longer constant. Δθ = ωt holds only when ω is constant. With uniform angular acceleration, use the average angular speed (ω_i + ω_f)/2, or one of the other equations of motion.

Working: ω_i = 1500 rev min⁻¹ × 2π rad/rev ÷ 60 s min⁻¹ = 157.1 rad s⁻¹; ω_f = 0. Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t = (157.1 rad s⁻¹/2)(20 s) = 1571 rad ≈ 1.57 × 10³ rad. (Check: α = −157.1/20 = −7.85 rad s⁻²; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt² = 3142 − 1571 = 1571 rad.)
items.specStatementText: that equations of motion for uniform angular acceleration can be used to predict the body’s angular position θ, angular displacement Δθ, angular speed ω and angular acceleration α, as given by Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t; ω_f = ω_i + αt; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt²; ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ
items.working: ω_i = 1500 rev min⁻¹ × 2π rad/rev ÷ 60 s min⁻¹ = 157.1 rad s⁻¹; ω_f = 0. Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t = (157.1 rad s⁻¹/2)(20 s) = 1571 rad ≈ 1.57 × 10³ rad. (Check: α = −157.1/20 = −7.85 rad s⁻²; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt² = 3142 − 1571 = 1571 rad.)

items.q: A wheel starts from rest and turns with a uniform angular acceleration of 3.0 rad s⁻². What is its angular speed at the moment it completes 8.0 revolutions?
items.correct: 17.4 rad s⁻¹
items.misconception: 6.93 rad s⁻¹
items.why:
Rotation rates are quoted in everyday life in revolutions per minute (engines, turntables, drills), and the radian feels like an arbitrary extra unit, so the 2π conversion is skipped or applied the wrong way. Convert every angle to radians and every rate to rad s⁻¹ before using Δθ = ..., ω = ..., L = Iω or E_k = ½Iω². Conversely, dividing by 2π gives revolutions, not radians.

Working: Δθ = 8.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 50.27 rad. ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ = 0 + 2(3.0 rad s⁻²)(50.27 rad) = 301.6 rad² s⁻². ω_f = 17.4 rad s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that equations of motion for uniform angular acceleration can be used to predict the body’s angular position θ, angular displacement Δθ, angular speed ω and angular acceleration α, as given by Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t; ω_f = ω_i + αt; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt²; ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ
items.random_wrong: 12.3 rad s⁻¹
items.working: Δθ = 8.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 50.27 rad. ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ = 0 + 2(3.0 rad s⁻²)(50.27 rad) = 301.6 rad² s⁻². ω_f = 17.4 rad s⁻¹.

items.q: A turntable starts from rest and rotates with uniform angular acceleration. During the first 2.0 s it turns through an angle θ. Through what angle does it turn during the next 2.0 s?
items.correct: 3θ, as the angle turned from rest reaches 4θ after 4.0 s
items.misconception: 2θ, as its angular speed at the end has doubled
items.why:
In uniform circular motion ω = Δθ/t exactly, so students apply the same division during angular acceleration, confusing the average with the final value. For uniform angular acceleration the average angular speed is (ω_i + ω_f)/2 = Δθ/t. Solve for ω_f from this, or use ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ.

Working: From rest with uniform α: θ(t) = ½αt². θ(2.0 s) = 2α = θ; θ(4.0 s) = 8α = 4θ. Angle turned between 2.0 s and 4.0 s = 4θ − θ = 3θ.
items.specStatementText: that equations of motion for uniform angular acceleration can be used to predict the body’s angular position θ, angular displacement Δθ, angular speed ω and angular acceleration α, as given by Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t; ω_f = ω_i + αt; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt²; ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ
items.random_wrong: θ, as equal time intervals give equal angles turned
items.working: From rest with uniform α: θ(t) = ½αt². θ(2.0 s) = 2α = θ; θ(4.0 s) = 8α = 4θ. Angle turned between 2.0 s and 4.0 s = 4θ − θ = 3θ.

items.q: A thin hoop and a uniform solid disc have the same mass and the same radius. Each rotates about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to its plane. Which has the greater moment of inertia about this axis?
items.correct: The hoop, as all its mass is at the maximum distance from the axis.
items.misconception: Neither, because bodies of equal mass have equal moments of inertia.
items.why: Moment of inertia is introduced as 'the rotational equivalent of mass', and students take the analogy literally. I = Σmr² weights each bit of mass by the square of its distance from the axis. Moving mass away from the axis increases I without changing the mass, and mass on the axis contributes nothing.
items.specStatementText: that the moment of inertia I depends on the distribution of mass of an extended body about an axis of rotation
items.random_wrong: The disc, since its mass is spread out over its whole area.

items.q: A uniform rod of mass M and length L can rotate either about an axis through its centre (I = ML²/12) or about an axis through one end (I = ML²/3), both perpendicular to the rod. The same resultant torque acts in each case. What is the ratio (angular acceleration about the centre)/(angular acceleration about the end)?
items.why:
Torque is force × distance, and students carry the unsquared distance across to moment of inertia; forgetting to square is also one of the commonest slips in any equation with r². Write I = Σmr² and square every distance before multiplying by the mass. A quick check: the unit must be kg m², not kg m.

Working: α = τ/I; same τ, so α_centre/α_end = I_end/I_centre = (ML²/3)/(ML²/12) = 12/3 = 4.00.
items.specStatementText: that the moment of inertia I depends on the distribution of mass of an extended body about an axis of rotation
items.working: α = τ/I; same τ, so α_centre/α_end = I_end/I_centre = (ML²/3)/(ML²/12) = 12/3 = 4.00.

items.q: A light rod of length 0.80 m rotates about an axis perpendicular to it through its midpoint. Small masses are fixed to the rod: 0.50 kg at end A, 0.20 kg at 0.20 m from end A, and 0.30 kg at end B. The centre of mass of the system is 0.12 m from the axis. What is the moment of inertia of the system about the axis?
items.correct: 1.4 × 10⁻¹ kg m²
items.misconception: 2.0 × 10⁻¹ kg m²
items.why:
Problems often locate masses by their distance from one end, and students substitute those numbers directly. Draw the axis and measure every r from it. Masses on opposite sides of the axis both contribute positively to I, because r² is positive.

Working: Distances from the axis at the midpoint: A at 0.40 m, the 0.20 kg mass at 0.40 − 0.20 = 0.20 m, B at 0.40 m. I = Σmr² = (0.50 kg)(0.40 m)² + (0.20 kg)(0.20 m)² + (0.30 kg)(0.40 m)² = 0.080 + 0.008 + 0.048 = 0.136 kg m² = 1.4 × 10⁻¹ kg m².
items.specStatementText: the moment of inertia for a system of point masses as given by I = Σmr²
items.random_wrong: 3.6 × 10⁻¹ kg m²
items.working: Distances from the axis at the midpoint: A at 0.40 m, the 0.20 kg mass at 0.40 − 0.20 = 0.20 m, B at 0.40 m. I = Σmr² = (0.50 kg)(0.40 m)² + (0.20 kg)(0.20 m)² + (0.30 kg)(0.40 m)² = 0.080 + 0.008 + 0.048 = 0.136 kg m² = 1.4 × 10⁻¹ kg m².

items.q: A system of small masses rotates about a fixed axis. Which single change doubles its moment of inertia about that axis?
items.correct: Doubling each mass, with all distances kept unchanged
items.misconception: Doubling the angular speed at which the system is rotating
items.why: Students conflate moment of inertia with angular momentum or kinetic energy, which do depend on angular speed, and with the everyday sense of 'inertia' as 'hard to stop'. I is a property of the body and its axis. How hard a body is to stop depends on its angular momentum L = Iω, which includes ω; I itself does not.
items.specStatementText: the moment of inertia for a system of point masses as given by I = Σmr²
items.random_wrong: Doubling each distance from the axis, with all masses unchanged

items.q: A flywheel of moment of inertia 0.50 kg m² is driven by a belt that exerts a tangential force of 40 N on its rim, 0.30 m from the axis. A frictional torque of 2.0 N m acts at the bearing, opposing the rotation. What is the angular acceleration of the flywheel?
items.correct: 20 rad s⁻²
items.misconception: 24 rad s⁻²
items.why:
The same error occurs in F = ma, where students substitute the applied force instead of the resultant force; problems often mention the friction torque as a separate detail. List every torque on the body with its sense and find the resultant before using τ = Iα. Opposing torques reduce the angular acceleration.

Working: Driving torque τ₁ = Fr = (40 N)(0.30 m) = 12 N m. Friction torque 2.0 N m in the opposite sense. Resultant τ = 12 − 2.0 = 10 N m. α = τ/I = (10 N m)/(0.50 kg m²) = 20 rad s⁻².
items.specStatementText: Newton’s second law for rotation as given by τ = Iα where τ is the average torque
items.random_wrong: 28 rad s⁻²
items.working: Driving torque τ₁ = Fr = (40 N)(0.30 m) = 12 N m. Friction torque 2.0 N m in the opposite sense. Resultant τ = 12 − 2.0 = 10 N m. α = τ/I = (10 N m)/(0.50 kg m²) = 20 rad s⁻².

items.q: A uniform disc of mass 3.0 kg and radius 0.20 m rotates at 240 revolutions per minute about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to its plane. For this axis, I = ½MR². What is the angular momentum of the disc?
items.correct: 1.51 kg m² s⁻¹
items.misconception: 3.02 kg m² s⁻¹
items.why:
I = mr² is the first formula learned and is easy to remember, so students apply it to every body, treating all the mass as if it were at the rim. Use the formula given for the specific shape. I = MR² is correct only for a thin hoop or ring, where all the mass really is at distance R.

Working: I = ½MR² = ½(3.0 kg)(0.20 m)² = 0.060 kg m². ω = 240 × 2π/60 = 25.13 rad s⁻¹. L = Iω = (0.060 kg m²)(25.13 rad s⁻¹) = 1.51 kg m² s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that an extended body rotating with an angular speed has an angular momentum L as given by L = Iω
items.random_wrong: 14.4 kg m² s⁻¹

items.q: A rigid body rotates about a fixed axis. Its angular momentum about that axis is determined by which quantities?
items.correct: Its moment of inertia about that axis and its angular speed
items.misconception: Its mass and the linear speed of its centre of mass
items.why: The word 'momentum' is shared, and students have met p = mv first, so they apply it to rotation, often using the speed of the centre of mass or of the rim. Keep linear and angular momentum separate. L = Iω (kg m² s⁻¹) describes rotation about an axis and is conserved when there is no resultant external torque; p = mv (kg m s⁻¹) describes the motion of the centre of mass.
items.specStatementText: that an extended body rotating with an angular speed has an angular momentum L as given by L = Iω
items.random_wrong: Its mass and angular speed, however the mass is arranged

items.q: A turntable of moment of inertia 0.020 kg m² rotates freely at 3.0 rad s⁻¹ on a frictionless bearing. A disc of moment of inertia 0.010 kg m², not rotating, is dropped onto it so that both share the same axis. Friction between them soon makes them rotate together. What is their common angular speed?
items.correct: 2.0 rad s⁻¹
items.misconception: 3.0 rad s⁻¹
items.why:
The rotational first law is taught for rigid bodies with fixed I, where constant L and constant ω amount to the same thing, and students keep the simpler statement about ω. The conserved quantity is L = Iω. For a rigid body with fixed I this means constant ω, but when I changes (a skater's arms, a disc dropped onto a turntable) ω must change so that the product stays the same.

Working: No external torque about the axis: L conserved. I₁ω₁ + I₂ω₂ = (I₁ + I₂)ω → (0.020)(3.0) + (0.010)(0) = (0.030)ω → ω = 0.060/0.030 = 2.0 rad s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that angular momentum remains constant unless the body is acted upon by a resultant torque
items.random_wrong: 1.5 rad s⁻¹
items.working: No external torque about the axis: L conserved. I₁ω₁ + I₂ω₂ = (I₁ + I₂)ω → (0.020)(3.0) + (0.010)(0) = (0.030)ω → ω = 0.060/0.030 = 2.0 rad s⁻¹.

items.q: A student sits on a stool that rotates freely about a vertical axis. She holds a 2.5 kg mass in each hand at 0.80 m from the axis and rotates at 2.0 rad s⁻¹. She then pulls both masses in to 0.20 m from the axis. Take the moment of inertia of the student and stool, without the masses, as a constant 2.0 kg m², and treat the masses as point masses. What is her new angular speed?
items.correct: 4.7 rad s⁻¹
items.misconception: 3.1 rad s⁻¹
items.why:
Students learn energy conservation as a universal principle and do not distinguish the total energy (always conserved) from the kinetic energy, which can be converted to or from other stores. Use conservation of angular momentum to find the new angular speed. Then check the kinetic energy: for a coupling with friction it falls; for a skater pulling in her arms it rises because her muscles do work.

Working: I_i = 2.0 + 2(2.5 kg)(0.80 m)² = 2.0 + 3.2 = 5.2 kg m². I_f = 2.0 + 2(2.5 kg)(0.20 m)² = 2.0 + 0.20 = 2.2 kg m². No external torque about the axis: I_iω_i = I_fω_f → ω_f = (5.2)(2.0)/2.2 = 4.7 rad s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that angular momentum remains constant unless the body is acted upon by a resultant torque
items.random_wrong: 4.0 rad s⁻¹
items.working: I_i = 2.0 + 2(2.5 kg)(0.80 m)² = 2.0 + 3.2 = 5.2 kg m². I_f = 2.0 + 2(2.5 kg)(0.20 m)² = 2.0 + 0.20 = 2.2 kg m². No external torque about the axis: I_iω_i = I_fω_f → ω_f = (5.2)(2.0)/2.2 = 4.7 rad s⁻¹.

items.q: A diver leaves a springboard rotating slowly with her body straight. In the air she pulls into a tight tuck and rotates much faster. Air resistance is negligible. Why does her angular speed increase?
items.correct: Her moment of inertia decreases while her angular momentum stays constant.
items.misconception: Pulling in her limbs exerts an external torque on her, which speeds her up.
items.why: For rigid bodies an external torque is indeed needed to change ω, and students extend this to bodies that change shape, treating internal forces as if they could produce an external torque. Pulling in the limbs involves internal forces, which exert equal and opposite torques on different parts of the body and cannot change its total angular momentum. The angular speed rises because I falls.
items.specStatementText: that angular momentum remains constant unless the body is acted upon by a resultant torque
items.random_wrong: Her weight exerts a torque about her centre of mass as she falls.

items.q: A wheel of moment of inertia 0.50 kg m² rotates counter-clockwise at 12 rad s⁻¹. A torque acts on it for 2.0 s, after which the wheel rotates clockwise at 4.0 rad s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the average torque on the wheel?
items.correct: 4.0 N m
items.misconception: 2.0 N m
items.why:
Angular speeds are quoted as positive numbers, and most worked examples involve a wheel speeding up or slowing down without reversing, where 'larger minus smaller' gives the right size of change. Before subtracting, choose a positive sense and give both values a sign. A wheel that reverses must first be brought to rest and then driven the other way, so the two sizes add: 12 + 4.0 = 16 rad s⁻¹.

Working: Take counter-clockwise as positive: ω_i = +12 rad s⁻¹, ω_f = −4.0 rad s⁻¹. ΔL = I(ω_f − ω_i) = (0.50 kg m²)(−16 rad s⁻¹) = −8.0 N m s. τ = ΔL/Δt = −8.0/2.0 = −4.0 N m, i.e. 4.0 N m clockwise.
items.specStatementText: that the action of a resultant torque constitutes an angular impulse ΔL as given by ΔL = τΔt = Δ(Iω)
items.random_wrong: 1.0 N m
items.working: Take counter-clockwise as positive: ω_i = +12 rad s⁻¹, ω_f = −4.0 rad s⁻¹. ΔL = I(ω_f − ω_i) = (0.50 kg m²)(−16 rad s⁻¹) = −8.0 N m s. τ = ΔL/Δt = −8.0/2.0 = −4.0 N m, i.e. 4.0 N m clockwise.

items.q: A wheel of moment of inertia 0.25 kg m² rotates counter-clockwise at 40 rad s⁻¹. A clockwise torque is then applied. A graph of the magnitude of this torque against time rises in a straight line from 0 at t = 0 to 4.0 N m at t = 0.50 s, stays at 4.0 N m until t = 1.50 s, then falls in a straight line to 0 at t = 2.0 s. No other torque acts. What is the angular speed of the wheel at t = 2.0 s?
items.correct: 16.0 rad s⁻¹
items.misconception: 64.0 rad s⁻¹
items.why:
Torque is taught as a scalar quantity in this course, and students treat 'scalar' as meaning 'always positive and simply added', losing the clockwise/counter-clockwise sense. Each torque has a sense. A friction torque opposing a driving torque reduces the resultant, and a torque opposite to the rotation reduces the angular momentum. Always decide the sense of each torque before combining them.

Working: Angular impulse = area under τ–t graph = ½(0.50 s)(4.0 N m) + (1.00 s)(4.0 N m) + ½(0.50 s)(4.0 N m) = 1.0 + 4.0 + 1.0 = 6.0 N m s (clockwise). Take counter-clockwise as positive: L_i = (0.25)(40) = 10 kg m² s⁻¹; L_f = 10 − 6.0 = 4.0 kg m² s⁻¹; ω_f = 4.0/0.25 = 16.0 rad s⁻¹, counter-clockwise.
items.specStatementText: that the action of a resultant torque constitutes an angular impulse ΔL as given by ΔL = τΔt = Δ(Iω)
items.random_wrong: 24.0 rad s⁻¹
items.working: Angular impulse = area under τ–t graph = ½(0.50 s)(4.0 N m) + (1.00 s)(4.0 N m) + ½(0.50 s)(4.0 N m) = 1.0 + 4.0 + 1.0 = 6.0 N m s (clockwise). Take counter-clockwise as positive: L_i = (0.25)(40) = 10 kg m² s⁻¹; L_f = 10 − 6.0 = 4.0 kg m² s⁻¹; ω_f = 4.0/0.25 = 16.0 rad s⁻¹, counter-clockwise.

items.q: A solid cylinder of mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.10 m is released from rest and rolls without slipping down a slope, descending a vertical height of 0.90 m. For the cylinder, I = ½MR². Take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and ignore energy dissipation. What is the speed of its centre of mass at the bottom of the slope?
items.correct: 3.4 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: 4.2 m s⁻¹
items.why:
Kinetic energy is learned for point particles, and the rule that an extended body may be treated as a mass at its centre of mass is applied to energy, where it misses the rotation. Include both terms. On a slope, a rolling body turns some of its lost gravitational potential energy into rotational kinetic energy, so it moves more slowly than a body sliding without friction.

Working: E_p lost = Mgh = (2.0 kg)(9.8 m s⁻²)(0.90 m) = 17.64 J. Rolling without slipping: ω = v/R. E_k = ½Mv² + ½(½MR²)(v/R)² = ¾Mv² = 1.5v² (in J, v in m s⁻¹). 1.5v² = 17.64 → v² = 11.76 → v = 3.4 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the kinetic energy of rotational motion as given by E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I.
items.random_wrong: 3.0 m s⁻¹
items.working: E_p lost = Mgh = (2.0 kg)(9.8 m s⁻²)(0.90 m) = 17.64 J. Rolling without slipping: ω = v/R. E_k = ½Mv² + ½(½MR²)(v/R)² = ¾Mv² = 1.5v² (in J, v in m s⁻¹). 1.5v² = 17.64 → v² = 11.76 → v = 3.4 m s⁻¹.

items.q: A skater spinning on ice with negligible friction pulls her arms in towards her body and spins faster. How do her angular momentum L and her rotational kinetic energy E_k change?
items.correct: L is unchanged; E_k increases, as she does work pulling her arms in.
items.misconception: L is unchanged; E_k is unchanged, since no external work is done.
items.why: Students learn energy conservation as a universal principle and do not distinguish the total energy (always conserved) from the kinetic energy, which can be converted to or from other stores. Use conservation of angular momentum to find the new angular speed. Then check the kinetic energy: for a coupling with friction it falls; for a skater pulling in her arms it rises because her muscles do work.
items.specStatementText: the kinetic energy of rotational motion as given by E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I.
items.random_wrong: L increases, because her mass is the same and she spins faster; E_k increases.

items.q: A thin hoop of mass 3.0 kg (I = MR²) and a solid cylinder of mass 1.0 kg (I = ½MR²), with equal radii, are released together from rest at the top of the same slope. Both roll without slipping. Which reaches the bottom first?
items.correct: The cylinder, as a smaller fraction of its E_k is rotational.
items.misconception: The hoop, because it is the heavier and so it accelerates faster.
items.why: The belief that heavier objects fall faster is one of the most widely documented misconceptions in mechanics, reinforced by everyday falling objects that are affected by air resistance. A greater weight gives a proportionally greater inertia, so mass cancels. Only the shape matters: for a hoop v² = gh, for a solid cylinder v² = 4gh/3.
items.specStatementText: the kinetic energy of rotational motion as given by E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I.
items.random_wrong: They arrive together, as the acceleration does not depend on mass.

items.q: A thin hoop (I = MR²) and a uniform solid disc (I = ½MR²) have the same mass M and the same radius R. Each is mounted on a frictionless axle through its centre, perpendicular to its plane, and is initially at rest. The same constant resultant torque τ is then applied to each. Which statement correctly compares their subsequent motion?
items.correct: After equal times the disc is turning faster, because its angular acceleration is twice that of the hoop.
items.misconception: The hoop has twice the angular acceleration of the disc, because its larger moment of inertia responds more to the torque.
items.why: Studies of students' reasoning about rotation report confusion between moment of inertia and torque, with I treated as a measure of turning effect rather than of resistance to angular acceleration. Moment of inertia plays the part of mass: it measures how hard it is to change the rotation. Larger I, smaller α for the same resultant torque.
items.specStatementText: Newton’s second law for rotation as given by τ = Iα where τ is the average torque
items.random_wrong: The two angular accelerations are equal, because the bodies have equal mass and the same torque acts on each.

items.q: Does the torque of a force depend on its direction as well as on its size and point of application?
items.correct: Yes. τ = Fr sin θ: the same force at the same point produces less torque the more closely it points along the line to the axis.
items.misconception: Torque is simply force × distance from the axis, whatever direction the force acts in.
items.why: The GCSE definition 'moment = force × distance' is learned with diagrams in which the force is always perpendicular to the lever, so the words 'perpendicular distance' are dropped and the distance to the point of application is used. The distance that matters is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action, r sin θ. Using r alone overestimates the torque of any force that is not at right angles to the lever.
items.specStatementText: the torque τ of a force about an axis as given by τ = Fr sin θ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When evaluating sin 70° on a calculator, what must be checked first?
items.correct: That the calculator is in degree mode. sin 70° = 0.940, whereas sin(70 rad) = 0.774.
items.misconception: The calculator's angle mode does not matter, so an angle given in degrees can be evaluated in radian mode.
items.why: Students switch their calculators to radian mode for circular-motion and rotation work and forget to switch back, and the wrong value still looks like a plausible sine between −1 and 1. An angle stated in degrees must be evaluated in degree mode (or converted to radians first). Check by estimating: sin 70° is close to 1, so a torque much smaller than Fr signals a mode error.
items.specStatementText: the torque τ of a force about an axis as given by τ = Fr sin θ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a beam balance when the forces on either side of the pivot are equal?
items.correct: Not in general. It balances when the total clockwise torque equals the total counter-clockwise torque; each force's distance from the pivot matters.
items.misconception: A beam balances when the downward forces on each side of the pivot are equal in size.
items.why: Many everyday balances (a symmetrical see-saw, a two-pan balance) have equal arms, so equal weights balance there and students generalise that forces, not torques, must match. The condition for rotational equilibrium is zero resultant torque. A small weight far from the pivot can balance a large weight close to it, which is how levers give mechanical advantage.
items.specStatementText: that bodies in rotational equilibrium have a resultant torque of zero
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If a body is in rotational equilibrium, must the resultant force on it be zero?
items.correct: No. Rotational equilibrium requires only zero resultant torque. A body can accelerate in a straight line without any angular acceleration, for example a box pulled along by a force through its centre of mass.
items.misconception: Rotational equilibrium automatically means the resultant force is zero as well.
items.why: In static problems both conditions hold together, so students merge them into a single idea of 'equilibrium' and do not see them as separate conditions. Translational equilibrium (zero resultant force) and rotational equilibrium (zero resultant torque) are independent. A body at rest needs both, but either can hold without the other.
items.specStatementText: that bodies in rotational equilibrium have a resultant torque of zero
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: After a torque is removed, does a body keep speeding up for a while?
items.correct: No. Angular acceleration exists only while an unbalanced torque acts (α = τ/I). Once the torque is removed, α = 0 immediately.
items.misconception: A torque gives the body a store of 'turning force' that keeps speeding it up until it is used up.
items.why: This is the rotational form of the impetus idea documented in mechanics research: a force is imagined to be transferred into the body and to run down gradually, rather than acting only while contact lasts. Torque is not stored. A rotating body stores angular momentum and kinetic energy, not torque; with no torque, its angular momentum and angular speed simply remain constant.
items.specStatementText: that an unbalanced torque applied to an extended, rigid body will cause angular acceleration
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If the angular acceleration of a body is zero, must it be at rest?
items.correct: No. Zero angular acceleration means the angular velocity is constant, which may be any value, including a large one.
items.misconception: Zero angular acceleration means zero angular velocity, so the body is not rotating.
items.why: Students confuse a quantity with its rate of change, as with velocity and acceleration in linear kinematics: 'no acceleration' is heard as 'no motion'. α = Δω/Δt. When α = 0 the angular velocity is not changing; it keeps whatever value it had when the torque stopped acting.
items.specStatementText: that an unbalanced torque applied to an extended, rigid body will cause angular acceleration
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can forces applied away from the centre of mass of a free body make its centre of mass accelerate when the resultant force on the body is zero?
items.correct: No. For linear motion the whole mass may be taken as concentrated at the centre of mass, so a_cm = F/M with F the resultant force, wherever the forces act. If the resultant force is zero the centre of mass does not accelerate; forces acting along different lines can still give a resultant torque.
items.misconception: A force applied away from the centre of mass moves the body as well as turning it, even when the forces on the body cancel.
items.why: Pushing a book near one edge across a table both slides it and turns it, so students link off-centre forces with both kinds of motion, and apply the resultant-force condition to the centre of mass only when the forces act at a single point. Use the resultant force to predict the motion of the centre of mass (F = Ma_cm) and the resultant torque to predict the rotation; the two are separate. A pair of equal, opposite forces acting along different lines has zero resultant force and a non-zero torque, so the body turns about its centre of mass while the centre of mass stays still.
items.specStatementText: that an unbalanced torque applied to an extended, rigid body will cause angular acceleration
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all points on a rotating rigid body have the same linear speed?
items.correct: No. They share the same angular velocity, but the linear speed v = ωr is greater for points further from the axis.
items.misconception: Every point of a rigid body moves together, so all points have the same linear speed.
items.why: Students know that a rigid body 'moves as one piece' and apply this to linear speed, which is true only for pure translation. In rotation each point travels round a circle of its own radius in the same time. A point twice as far from the axis travels twice as far per revolution, so it has twice the linear speed.
items.specStatementText: that the rotation of a body can be described in terms of angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does ω = v/r mean that points further from the axis of a rigid body have smaller angular velocity?
items.correct: No. For points on one rigid body ω is fixed; v increases in proportion to r, so v/r is the same for every point.
items.misconception: Because ω = v/r, a point further from the axis has a smaller angular velocity.
items.why: Students read an equation as a proportionality between two of its quantities while silently holding the third constant, here assuming v is the same for both points. Before reading proportions from ω = v/r, decide which quantity is fixed. For a rigid body ω is the same everywhere, so it is v that changes with r.
items.specStatementText: that the rotation of a body can be described in terms of angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What sign does α have for a wheel that is slowing down?
items.correct: Opposite to the sign of ω. Taking the direction of rotation as positive, a slowing wheel has negative α.
items.misconception: Angular acceleration is always positive, so the magnitude of α is substituted as a positive number even when the wheel slows.
items.why: The word 'acceleration' suggests speeding up, and the angular equations are often taught with examples of bodies starting from rest, so the sign convention is never practised. Choose a positive sense of rotation and keep to it. A deceleration is a negative α, and Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt² then gives a smaller angle than ω_i t, not a larger one.
items.specStatementText: that equations of motion for uniform angular acceleration can be used to predict the body’s angular position θ, angular displacement Δθ, angular speed ω and angular acceleration α, as given by Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t; ω_f = ω_i + αt; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt²; ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ, is there a factor of 2 or ½?
items.correct: A factor of 2: ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ.
items.misconception: The equation is ω_f² = ω_i² + αΔθ, or the ½ from Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt² belongs here, so the factor 2 is dropped.
items.why: The four equations of motion contain several similar-looking factors (½ and 2), and students who memorise them rather than derive them mix them up. The equation follows from eliminating t between ω_f = ω_i + αt and Δθ = ((ω_i + ω_f)/2)t, which gives ω_f² − ω_i² = 2αΔθ. Check it with units and with a simple case.
items.specStatementText: that equations of motion for uniform angular acceleration can be used to predict the body’s angular position θ, angular displacement Δθ, angular speed ω and angular acceleration α, as given by Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t; ω_f = ω_i + αt; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt²; ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the angle turned in a time interval the same as the angular position reached at its end?
items.correct: No. The angular position θ is measured from the starting reference; the angular displacement Δθ in an interval is the difference between the positions at its end and its start.
items.misconception: The angle turned in a later interval is the angle given by the equation for the whole time from the start.
items.why: The equations of motion are usually applied from t = 0, so students do not practise subtracting the angle already turned, and position and displacement are used interchangeably. To find the angle turned between t₁ and t₂, find the angular position at each time and subtract: Δθ = θ(t₂) − θ(t₁).
items.specStatementText: that equations of motion for uniform angular acceleration can be used to predict the body’s angular position θ, angular displacement Δθ, angular speed ω and angular acceleration α, as given by Δθ = ((ω_f + ω_i)/2)t; ω_f = ω_i + αt; Δθ = ω_i t + ½αt²; ω_f² = ω_i² + 2αΔθ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does spreading mass over a larger area always give a larger moment of inertia?
items.correct: No. What matters is the distance of the mass from the axis. A hoop, with all its mass at the rim, has a larger moment of inertia than a solid disc of the same mass and radius, even though the disc's mass covers more area.
items.misconception: The more spread out over its area the mass of a body is, the larger its moment of inertia.
items.why: Students are told that 'spread-out' mass increases I and interpret 'spread out' as 'filling more area' rather than 'further from the axis'. Consider where the mass lies relative to the axis. A solid disc has much of its mass near the centre, so for the same mass and radius its I (½MR²) is half that of a hoop (MR²).
items.specStatementText: that the moment of inertia I depends on the distribution of mass of an extended body about an axis of rotation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the moment of inertia be found by placing all the mass at the centre of mass?
items.correct: No. The centre-of-mass model works for linear motion only. For rotation, I = Σmr² depends on the distance of each mass from the axis, and is in general larger than M × (distance from the axis to the centre of mass)².
items.misconception: Because the mass of an extended body may be taken as concentrated at its centre of mass, I = M × (distance from the axis to the centre of mass)².
items.why: The guidance rightly says the mass may be taken as concentrated at the centre of mass for linear motion, and students extend this useful rule to rotation. Use I = Σmr² with every mass at its own distance. For a body rotating about an axis through its centre of mass the centre-of-mass model would even give I = 0, which is clearly wrong.
items.specStatementText: the moment of inertia for a system of point masses as given by I = Σmr²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a force be substituted directly for torque in τ = Iα?
items.correct: No. The torque of a force applied at distance r at right angles to the radius is τ = Fr. The force must be multiplied by its distance from the axis.
items.misconception: Force and torque are interchangeable, so a tangential force F can be used as the torque in τ = Iα.
items.why: Torque is often described informally as a 'turning force', which suggests it is a kind of force measured in newtons. Torque (N m) and force (N) are different quantities with different units. Convert a tangential force to a torque with τ = Fr before using τ = Iα.
items.specStatementText: Newton’s second law for rotation as given by τ = Iα where τ is the average torque
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the angular momentum of a body determined by the torque acting on it at that moment?
items.correct: No. L = Iω depends on the present moment of inertia and angular speed. Torque determines how fast L is changing (τ = ΔL/Δt), not its value.
items.misconception: A body has large angular momentum when a large torque is acting on it, and no angular momentum once the torque stops.
items.why: This is the rotational form of 'motion implies force': students link the amount of motion to the cause currently acting rather than to the change in motion. A flywheel spinning freely with no torque on it keeps its angular momentum. Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, just as force is the rate of change of linear momentum.
items.specStatementText: that an extended body rotating with an angular speed has an angular momentum L as given by L = Iω
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When two coaxial bodies are coupled so that they rotate together, is the final angular speed the average of their initial angular speeds?
items.correct: Only if their moments of inertia are equal. In general, conservation of angular momentum gives ω = (I₁ω₁ + I₂ω₂)/(I₁ + I₂).
items.misconception: The combined angular speed is the average of the two initial angular speeds.
items.why: Averaging is an intuitive way to combine two values, and it happens to be right for equal moments of inertia, the case most often shown. Weight each angular speed by its moment of inertia: total angular momentum before = total after. A light disc dropped on a heavy turntable slows it only slightly.
items.specStatementText: that angular momentum remains constant unless the body is acted upon by a resultant torque
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the weight of a freely rotating diver exert a torque about her centre of mass?
items.correct: No. Her weight acts at her centre of mass, so its line of action passes through that point and its torque about it is zero. Her angular momentum about her centre of mass is therefore constant in the air.
items.misconception: As the diver falls, her weight exerts a torque that makes her spin faster.
items.why: Students see the diver both falling and spinning faster, and link the two because gravity is the one obvious force acting. For linear motion her mass may be taken as concentrated at her centre of mass, so gravity accelerates that point downward, but it exerts no torque about it. Any change in her angular speed must come from a change in her moment of inertia.
items.specStatementText: that angular momentum remains constant unless the body is acted upon by a resultant torque
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is angular impulse the same as torque?
items.correct: No. Angular impulse is torque multiplied by the time for which it acts, ΔL = τΔt (unit N m s); torque (N m) is the rate of change of angular momentum.
items.misconception: The change in angular momentum is equal to the torque, so the time for which the torque acts does not matter.
items.why: The same confusion between impulse and force occurs in linear mechanics, and both are described informally as 'how hard something is pushed'. The same change of angular momentum can be produced by a large torque for a short time or a small torque for a long time. Divide the change in angular momentum by the time to find the average torque.
items.specStatementText: that the action of a resultant torque constitutes an angular impulse ΔL as given by ΔL = τΔt = Δ(Iω)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the change in angular momentum equal to the final angular momentum?
items.correct: Only if the body starts from rest. In general ΔL = L_final − L_initial, so the initial angular momentum must be included.
items.misconception: The angular impulse gives the final angular momentum (or the final angular speed) directly.
items.why: Many worked examples start from rest, where the change and the final value coincide, so students stop distinguishing them. Write ΔL = I(ω_f − ω_i) with signs for the senses of rotation, and solve for ω_f; do not equate the angular impulse with I ω_f.
items.specStatementText: that the action of a resultant torque constitutes an angular impulse ΔL as given by ΔL = τΔt = Δ(Iω)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the angular impulse of a varying torque be found from the maximum torque multiplied by the time?
items.correct: No. The angular impulse is the average torque multiplied by the time, which is the area under the torque–time graph; using the peak value overestimates it.
items.misconception: The angular impulse of a torque that varies is its maximum value multiplied by the time for which it acts.
items.why: The equation ΔL = τΔt is learned with constant torques, and the qualification in the guide that τ is the average torque is overlooked. When the torque varies, find the area under the torque–time graph, splitting it into triangles and rectangles where it is made of straight lines.
items.specStatementText: that the action of a resultant torque constitutes an angular impulse ΔL as given by ΔL = τΔt = Δ(Iω)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is rotational kinetic energy Iω² or ½Iω²?
items.correct: ½Iω², the rotational counterpart of ½mv².
items.misconception: Rotational kinetic energy is Iω², without the ½.
items.why: Students remember that I replaces m and ω replaces v but drop the numerical factor, especially when the ½ in I = ½MR² is also present and the halves become confused. E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I. Check by analogy with ½mv² and by the units: kg m² × (rad s⁻¹)² = J.
items.specStatementText: the kinetic energy of rotational motion as given by E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all objects released together on a slope reach the bottom together?
items.correct: Only if they slide without friction or have the same shape factor I/MR². Rolling bodies with a larger fraction of energy in rotation are slower.
items.misconception: All objects accelerate down a slope at the same rate, so they arrive together, just as all objects fall together in a vacuum.
items.why: Students correctly learn that acceleration in free fall does not depend on mass and over-generalise this to rolling, where the distribution of mass matters. The mass cancels, but the mass distribution does not. Compare the fractions of kinetic energy that are rotational: the body with the smaller fraction gains more speed.
items.specStatementText: the kinetic energy of rotational motion as given by E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a larger moment of inertia make a rolling body roll down a slope faster?
items.correct: No. A larger moment of inertia (relative to MR²) means more of the energy goes into rotation, so the body gains less speed.
items.misconception: A body with a larger moment of inertia has more 'inertia' to keep it going, so it rolls faster.
items.why: The everyday meaning of inertia as a tendency to keep moving is confused with momentum, so more inertia is read as more 'go'. Inertia resists changes in motion, including speeding up. For the same loss of E_p, a hoop (I = MR²) gains less translational speed than a solid cylinder (I = ½MR²).
items.specStatementText: the kinetic energy of rotational motion as given by E_k = ½Iω² = L²/2I.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In τ = Fr, from which point is the distance r measured when a beam turns about a pivot that is not at its end?
items.correct: From the pivot (the axis of rotation) to the line of action of the force. Positions quoted from one end of the beam must first be converted to distances from the pivot.
items.misconception: The distance used in a torque is measured from the end of the beam where positions are given, not from the pivot.
items.why: Beam problems locate forces by their distance from one end, and in many introductory examples the pivot is at that end, so the given positions are the distances. Students keep substituting the given positions when the pivot is elsewhere. Mark the pivot first and measure every distance from it. A force at the pivot has no torque about it, and forces on opposite sides of the pivot turn the beam in opposite senses.
items.specStatementText: that bodies in rotational equilibrium have a resultant torque of zero
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a second force balances the turning effect of a force, is the torque of the first force zero?
items.correct: No. The torque of a force, τ = Fr sin θ, depends only on that force, where it acts and its direction. Other forces can make the resultant torque zero, but they do not change the torque of this force.
items.misconception: When another force balances it, a force's own torque becomes zero; the torque of one force and the resultant torque are the same thing.
items.why: In equilibrium problems a balanced body is described as having 'no torque' on it, meaning no resultant torque, and everyday phrases such as 'the turning effect is cancelled' suggest that each individual turning effect disappears. Keep the torque of one force separate from the resultant torque. On a balanced see-saw each child's weight still has a torque about the pivot; the two torques are equal in size and opposite in sense, so their sum is zero.
items.specStatementText: the torque τ of a force about an axis as given by τ = Fr sin θ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
